- I like that you're talking
about having confidence
in the AI tool and what it can produce

and that it actually
reflects what you want to go
into the physical product.
- Yeah.

And you know, you didn't
ask, but I'll say,

disruptors often come
from outside the industry
or peripheral to the industry.

I wonder sometimes whether
you're 10, 15 years from now

that the preferred tool
of print circuit design,

whether that will be one
of the legacy companies

or whether that's going to
come from somebody, you know,
coming in from a different angle
with a different perspective

and not beholden to a
gazillion lines of code
that they're trying to build on top of.
(Zach laughing)
I don't know.

And I'm not saying one
is right or one is wrong.

It's just one of those
things I kind of kick around
and wonder sometimes
when I don't have anything else to do,
which is just not often enough.
(upbeat music)
- Hello everyone,

and welcome to the
"Altium OnTrack" podcast.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.
Today, we're talking with Mike Buteau,

President of the Printed
Circuit Engineering Association.
If you're familiar with PCEA,

you know that they put
on two very big shows
in the US that is PCB East and PCB West.
Very happy to have Mike on today
to talk about a new show, PCB Detroit.
Mike, thank you so much for joining us.
- [Mike] Thank you, Zach.
It's a pleasure to be here.
- So PCEA was started not that long ago,
I think back in 2020.
So it's a pretty young organization.
Maybe if you could,

tell us some of the progress
with PCEA around membership

and how many people have
taken some of your courses,
things like that.
- Right, well, it's almost,
I'm not quite sure even where to start.

So we have individual membership
and corporate membership.
Individual membership is free,
and that continues to grow every year.

Much of the genesis of
PCEA, as you mentioned,
came just about five years ago.
And in that time the emphasis has been

on the individual membership
kind of growing the industry
and the profession from the ground up.

So, you know, we are agnostic
when it comes to companies

and software, and we are very
much vested in, you know,
how can we advance the professional career
of circuit board designers, engineers,
fabricators, and assemblers.
So we are chapter-based,

and I know that folks
are probably familiar
with how that works.
We have local chapters all over the place
and they will meet sometimes in person,
sometimes online, sometimes it's a hybrid,

where they Maybe meet
once a year physically,
and then they do everything else online.

The meetings kind of run
the gamut of, you know,

they might be purely
technical, like the chapter,

the Portland chapter, which
you've been involved in.
You know, they have
a one-hour online meeting every month.

In fact, the next one will
be, it's like the third,

usually the third or fourth
Thursday of the month,
and they have a guest speaker,

and it's really kind of
a technical-oriented talk
for about 50 minutes,

and then they'll spend the
last 10 minutes just talking

about things that they're
working on locally.
And that chapter, for instance,
has a round robin that they're doing

looking at data transfer
in different formats.
And so it's really pretty sophisticated,
in how they've approached networking
and tech transfer.

You have other chapters that
are primarily in person,
like San Diego.
They'll meet three

or four times a year
at a central location,
and they always have a guest speaker.
There's maybe a couple hours,

and they'll have some
snacks and things like that.

And there's a lot of
networking, and you know,
also some good technical content.

And then you have other
chapters like Boston,

which is kind of a hybrid
where we'll do some things
in person, some things online.

We're trying to get
people together, right?
Which as you know,

is harder and harder to do
in the post-Covid time frame.

So that sort of encapsulates
what we're doing
from a membership standpoint.

Corporate membership
continues to grow every year.
We just started offering that in 2023.
We're up to 33, 34 corporate members now.
They run the gamut

of major ECAD companies
like Siemens and Cadence.
You have fabricators.
You have suppliers,
both on the fabrication and assembly side.
So you know, there's manufacturers,
there's equipment and software developers.
It's kind of the gamut.
And we see that as continuing to grow,

and really what that does is
it helps to offset the cost
of the programming

so that we can continue to
provide the bulk of our content
for free to the individual members.

So that's what's going on
from a membership standpoint.
And then, you know,
some of our other events continue to grow.
I mean, we looked at the number
of engagements we had last year,
and it was on the order of 4.6 million,

which was up by over a million
over the previous year.
So our reach continues to expand.

- Yeah, you mentioned a
lot about content delivery,

and I think that's that's
happening in a few formats.
There's, what is it?

"Printed Circuit Design &
Fab" and "Circuits Assembly,"
so magazines that are being used
to deliver technical articles,

but then there's also
professional training.
- Yes, that's right.
So we acquired an organization last year
called the, what was a PCE-EDU,
and what we've done in that time,
actually it was in 2023,

but last year was the
first year that we had it
completely under the umbrella of PCEA.
And so most folks will recognize

that for the certified printed
circuit designer curriculum,

there's a certification exam
that goes along with that.

But the meat of it is a
40-hour training program
that will teach you soup to nuts,
everything about printed circuit design.
And so, you know, we go over, you know,
it's almost 80 different topic areas,

and it's intended for folks
who are new in the industry,
but it's also intended

for folks who may have been
doing things for 15 or 20 years,

but need to kind of
refresh on certain areas
because we'll cover a lot about materials.
There's information about fabrication

and assembly process and
how they relate to design,

how they might affect
your design decisions.
Because as you know, you do this,

it's really, there's no
necessarily right way
or only way to do something.
It's often a matter of trade-offs.

And I think that the instructors
that teach that course,

and in particular the five
folks who developed it,

they're all people whose names
are synonymous with design
and design engineering.
Rick Hartley, Susy Webb, Mike Creeden,
Gary Ferrari, Steph Chavez.
They really, I think, got to the core
of what it means to take all
of this sometimes disparate information
and figure out what the trade-offs are
and what you can live with
and what you can't for a given design,
and convey that in a conversational way
to a prospective designer.
You know, it's not an overload on theory.

It's not so basic that
folks will just say,
"Hey, look, I've done all this."
We do surveys at the end of each class,

and there's even, regardless
of whether they're new
or 20 years in the industry,
it always comes back,

"Wow, okay, this really opened
my eyes to this or that."

So that's a big part of what
we've been doing lately.
And it's definitely a growth area.

We all know that the need
for training is everywhere.

There's not a lot at the
university or college level

and certainly not at the high
school level when it comes

to teaching circuit board
design and engineering.

And so it's up to third
parties to do that,
whether it's your employer
or whether it's companies like PCEA.

We are starting to partner
with different organizations

to license that program and
try to expand the reach,
because there is demand
at the college level now really coming
from the grassroots, right?
From students up, for learning skills,
coming out with a certification.
And you know,

if I can talk a little
bit about our partnership
with Wayne State,
I can go into some more detail on that.

- Yeah, I definitely
want to hear about that.
But I do want to underscore, I think,
one thing about

the Printed Circuit Engineering
Association curriculum
that I found really insightful,

because I think when you look
at a lot of design trainings,

especially if they're
offered by the EDA companies,
they start to become really tool-focused.

And obviously if you're
going to design something,
you have to use software.

And so, it's important
to learn the software.
And they're tool providers,

so of course they're going to
teach you how to use software.
But the thing about the PCEA curriculum

is that I think it comes more
from like a DFM perspective

and it gets you to focus
on, if you can't produce it,

it doesn't matter what you
do in the design software,
none of it matters.

- Well, you're preaching
to the choir here, Zach.
(Zach laughing)
I couldn't agree more.
And in fact, yesterday we had a webinar,
our Kansas City chapter just kicked off

with a special webinar
on design for assembly.
But it was brought to us by Dale Lee,
who's an engineer at Plexus.
And as Dale's fond of saying,
"It's really not designed for assembly
or design for manufacturing,
it's manufacturing by design."
And for example,
designers could put a 45-degree buried via

inside 60 layers of
board or whatever, right?
You could trick the machine,
the software, to do anything you want.

But then you send that
over to manufacturing,
and they can't build it.
And so what's the point?

So it really is understanding
what the constraints are
at the fabrication and assembly level,
and then communicating them back to design

so that the designer can
best match the intent
and functionality of the end product
to what is actually manufacturable

at a reasonable cost and
at a reasonable yield.

- Yeah, that's where you get
a lot of those trade-offs.

And I think that's where a
lot of design guidelines,
especially pushed in PDFs on the Internet,
a lot of them are teaching

or they're trying to teach
you how to build a Ferrari.

And I think the real art
is building a Toyota.

- Right, so I mean we
see this more and more.

Think about all the IoT
devices that are out there.
I mean you probably have a half-dozen
on your desk right now,

and probably who knows
how many in your house.
All your Alexas, and your Nest,
and your Rings, and so forth.

Those aren't 10, 12,
16-layer boards. (chuckles)

They're two and maybe
four layer boards, okay?

We are seeing a lot of
that kind of technology.
And I want to go back
to something that you mentioned earlier
about the training in itself.
It is agnostic to the tool.
The Altiums and companies like that,

you know, the software
developers provide training
that is specific to their tool,

because that's what their
customer wants to use.
We're coming at it from a different angle,

which is that we're not
teaching the tool training.

Altium and its competitors
are more than capable
of doing that.

What we are teaching are
great design concepts

so that you understand
what all goes into that.
As you mentioned, the DFM,

you understand what all
those constraints are,

and you're able to make those
design decisions in real time.
- Definitely, definitely.
Now a moment ago you mentioned some work
that PCEA is doing with Wayne State.
So I'd love to hear some more about that.
- Right, so thanks for reminding me.
So Wayne State is actually

the third-largest public
institution in Michigan.

It's 28,000 or so undergrad
students, I believe.
It's located in Detroit,
and we've been partnering with them now
for the last couple years.
It really kind of took off last year

where they have some government
grants that are helping
to underwrite some programming.
And so they had asked us to come in

and give a tailored
version of our CPCD course
to their students.

That then was parlayed
into a semester-long class.

And Wayne State is the
first official licensee

from the academic level
of the CPCD program.

We do have licensees that are
third-party training centers.
And so they have,
they're offering the full 40-hour class
taught by one of our instructors,
plus they have added some labs.

They're doing a facility
tour of a fabricator
and an assembler.

The students will design
their own Arduino board,

and the certification exam
will be the final exam.

So the students will walk out
of there with the full class,

in addition to some hands-on
practical experience,

and hopefully they will have
a certification to boot.

Wayne State was hoping
they would get nine,
maybe 10 students in this first class.
They got 23.
So they've already,
I think it's resonating with students
who are interested in engineering,
interested in electronics,
and interested in hardware.
A lot of engineers, as you know,
they might gravitate towards software.
We obviously have a little bit
of a bias toward the physical space,
and it's great to see there's

so much interest at that
particular university.

We've been in discussions
with several other schools
over the past 12 to 18 months

and with one large public
private consortium about, again,
kind of tailoring the content
so that it is, I think,
efficient for their particular audience.

For example, one of this
public private consortium

has a large audience
of high school students

through a community, or,
sorry, through a network

of community colleges that
they're affiliated with
all around the country, all around the US,
and so we are looking
at providing a stripped-down version

of the CPCD program to high
schoolers all over the country
at no cost to them.
And if you want to get folks interested
in this career, right?

I think you need to hit
them as early as possible.
Waiting until college

or post-college might even
be a little bit too late.

You know, I'd like to start
getting into the high school
and the even earlier phase,

because as a trusted
colleague of mine once said,

"The future of the printed
circuit board design industry

is right now playing
Minecraft in the basement."

And I firmly believe that.
(Zach laughing)
- I would 100% agree.
And I actually think back

to my childhood playing
computer games with my dad

and every so often having
to pull the computer open
and replace something or repair something.
And I think that was my first encounter
with this green piece of plastic
that he called a circuit board.
(Mike laughing)
And he didn't know what it did.
I didn't know what it did.

But who knew that 30 years
later I'd be doing this.
- Right, I mean, it teaches you,
Minecraft specifically,

but a lot of computer games
today teach you to think in 3D
and they allow you to be very creative.
So, I know that you have a young one now,

and they're probably a
couple years away still
from sitting on your lap
and designing their own world, right?
But it will happen.

And the neat thing is
watching how they take an idea
and make it reality, right?
So I go and I talk to middle schools,
and I do this very willingly,
because in the first,
I always start the conversation with,

"How many of you have
parents who have told you
that you're playing too many video games?"

And like every hand in
the room will go up.
And my response is,

"I'm here to tell you
to play more." (laughs)

You know, not only
because you're customers,
every console you buy, right,
has lots of boards in it,

but because there is a chance
that instead of going off
and designing an app,
that you might be interested
in the hardware that supports all that.
And I might be able

to teach you a little bit
about why that's important
and why, how far we can come,
if we just are open to dreaming, right?
Think about what your first TV looked like
when you're a little kid,

and then look what your
TV looks like today.

Showing pictures of that is
really all they need to know.

You know, they see how far
things have come in just 20 years
and it starts to dawn on the kids that,

hey, look, you know what,
maybe I could do this,
and maybe I'd like to do this.
- You know, one way I've often felt

that we can more effectively
reach maybe that older part
of the young demographic,
maybe late high school,
early university that might think

that software is the way
to go is through embedded.

And you mentioned that the
students at Wayne State,
they're building their own Arduino board,

they're probably in another
class where they're going
to learn to program that Arduino board.
So it all kind of comes together
and it gives them a path

and a way to kind of go in
either direction, right?
They can go into software,
they can go purely into hardware,
or they can go into systems design
where they're doing a little bit of both.
- Absolutely.
And by the way, I mean, I know this comes
across as a little bit heavy-handed
against the software guys, and in fact,
it's really the other way around.
I mean, we need them badly, right?
We need the Altiums

and companies like that to
keep improving the tools,
make them more user friendly,
make them more functional,

you know, help to make
them more available, right?

So that the folks in the
next generation can dream
of a product that they'd like to see
and then actually sit down at their laptop
and design it and then send it

to maybe some kind of
additive processing machine,
and make it reality just like that.

I mean, my life in this
industry goes back 30 years.
And the folks at the MIT Media Lab,

which is kind of like
their Innovation Lab,
have been talking about this forever.

The idea that a person
could dream of something

and without any real engineering
skill or design background,
could sit down at a computer,
and map it out, and then push a button
and have it created at their desktop.

We're not there yet, but
we're getting closer.
- Yeah, every little advance, right?

I mean, I guess maybe if
we all get neural links,
we'll be able to do that a lot easier.
(Mike and Zach laughing)
- Hey, my wife's a neuropsychologist,

and so that part kind of scares
me a little bit. (laughs)
- Okay. (laughs)
That's a deep topic for sure.

Maybe getting into something
a little more shallow,
during the introduction to this podcast,

I mentioned that there are
shows that PCEA puts on.
Obviously, you know,

two of the biggest are
PCB West and PCB East.
And I think, you know,
aside from a couple other industry shows,

those are really the
two most important shows
for people who do PCB design.
But now, I guess,

thanks to your work with
Wayne State University,

there's been another
show that has just come

across my feed on LinkedIn,
which is PCB Detroit.
And this was really interesting,

because I periodically
get asked by people,
"When are they going to do PCB Kansas?"
Or something like that, right?
They want a PCB Midwest,

or they want a PCB South,
or something like that.

So all of a sudden there's
this PCB Detroit show.

So if you could just tell
us a little bit about this.
- Right, so we do get that as well.

PCB West has been around
for more than 30 years.

That's the show in the
Silicon Valley every year.
PCB East was founded in the late 1990s.
And then after, really after 9/11,
we kind of said, "Okay,

maybe we should just
consolidate everything
and sort of focus on the West Coast show."
The industry went through some bumps.
A few years ago, we brought that back,
and that's been growing each year.
It almost doubled in size last year.

And so we like the
trajectory of that show.

But one of the things
that we noticed is that
as the industry has become more, you know,
I don't want to say smaller,
because it's really not smaller
in terms of the number of people employed
or anything like that,
but it's absolutely compartmentalized,

and the ability for folks to
travel is somewhat limited,

and especially, you know,
folks from the East Coast

or even the Midwest to
spend a day on the plane,

go out to California for
four days, and then fly back.
This is another day on the plane.

And oftentimes there's not a
lot of back support for them.
So that while they're gone,
their work is just increasing.

Everything that they've left
behind continues to pile up.
So getting away is a problem.
The time spent traveling is a problem,
the funds are a problem.
Everything is a constraint.

So we looked at the
demographics of our shows,

and we noticed that
there was sort of a hole
in the middle Midwest, and we said,
"Let's try this."
We had the partnership with Wayne State.

So this June, June 2nd
and 3rd to be specific,

we are introducing a
two-day technical conference
on the campus of Wayne State.
And we think of it

as sort of a smaller version
of PCB East or PCB West.

Instead of 75 or 125 hours
of training, you know,
it's two days, two sessions.

So it's more in the order of
about 25 hours of training.

But you'll see a lot of the
speakers that you're used to.

You know, Rick Hartley,
Susy Webb, Dan Beeker,

Ethan Pierce, Dave Lackey,
Bob Carter, you know,
Steph Chavez, those are some of them.
And you know, the technical program will

sort of cover the gamut of
introductory to advanced topics,
things like controlling noise, right,

which is a staple of
all of our conferences,
because it's just so important.

But we'll get into flex
and rigid flex materials.
We'll look at HDI via design.
We'll look at cost drivers for PCBs.

There's a talk on using AI
in hardware and PCB design.

So we're kind of pushing
the envelope in some areas

and then maintaining kind
of the good tutorial,
basic information in others.

And there's going to be a
small exhibit with that.
It's just tabletops.
There's only room for about 14 companies.
I think it might already be sold out

or if it's not, we have
maybe one booth left.
And the focus of this really will be
on hitting that local audience,

which is much more vibrant
than I think people realize.
And it's not just automotive either.

Leveraging what's going on
in the state of Michigan,
which is another great untold story.
The state has identified some areas
for workforce development

in electronics, semiconductors,
mobility are three of them.
Three of their four key areas,

all of those are related
to what we're doing.
And so with the state backing,
with the emphasis on the local ecosystem,
there's probably 40 to 50 EMS companies,
all the big automotive companies,

lots of industrial work
is done there as well.
It's really a thriving,

if underrated and probably
underserved ecosystem.
And we're looking forward to that event.

- So one thing I'm wondering
with university involvement,
sometimes when universities are involved,

there's an opportunity,
I think, for some groups
at the university to maybe present some

of the innovative things
they're doing, research,

present their lab, what
they're doing with students,
those kinds of things.

Is that going to be
happening at PCB Detroit?
- So not at this one,

although we have extended
an invite to many

of the local universities
and community colleges

and some of the extension
schools to join us at the event.

And we actually have a very
economical student rate.

But what you're saying is
very interesting, right,
because there is a bit of a disconnect
between what's going on in industry
and what goes on in academia.

Whereas what Wayne
State is doing is really
where the rubber meets the road,

where they're using
industry-developed curricula
for their classes.
That's not true everywhere.

One of the things that I
liked about the last few years

in PCEA is looking around
and seeing the number

of schools that actually
are trying to pull people

from industry in and teach
real life knowledge and skills.
You know, Austin Community College,
Rochester Institute of Technology,
University of Alabama,
even Stanford does it.

So it's not just schools
that are primarily looked at

as being engineers-first
or anything like that.

It's not just vocational
or community colleges.
It really does run the gamut.
But one of the things that we have to do,
and this is an area of focus for me
over the next year or so,

is to hopefully make the
universities understand

that not only is there a
demand from their own students

for certification and
for hands-on training,
but that sometimes what they think happens

in industry doesn't
actually happen that way.
Our chairman Steph Chavez

and I had an interesting
conversation with a fellow,

a professor at North Carolina
State University last fall.

And this is a guy that's
heavily involved in IEEE.

He's very smart, and I
don't want to dismiss any

of the things that he was
trying to get across to us,

but his opinion was that colleges
aren't there for teaching,
that that's for somebody else,
and that that might have been true
for him as a research-first professor,
but it's not really true everywhere.
And it's not really what most
of the students are asking for today.
It's one of those things where we,

as a training organization
that has a curriculum,
if we want to get it into universities,
we need to convince them

that there's something else
that they need to take out.
Because you know this, right?

Because you're as educated
as anybody that I know.

Every time we add
another class, (chuckles)
that's more time you have

to spend finishing your
Bachelor's, Master's, PhD.

So you really need to have
something else come out

or it needs to represent a
different potential career path

to be convincing to the
institutions to implement it.
That's a much harder sell, we found.
- Yeah, I mean,

it's either that or they
just add it to the program
and then it languishes there forever.
And then it never actually gets offered.
And then, you know, what's the point?
You go through all this work for nothing.

You know, that was something
that I actually experienced,
back when I was working in Portland State.

- Right, so what we've seen
is that at some schools,
I'm not going to pick on anybody,
but there's some colleges that have tried
to implement, recently,
design, PCB design classes,

and they've plucked people
out of the nuclear sub-world,
not a joke, okay,
where they were in operations and said,

"Well, you know something
about technology.
You teach this."

And those folks have come
to our conferences and said,
"Okay, teach me about design,

because I need to go teach
this to students." (laughs)
Okay, good luck.
(Zach and Mike laughing)
It just doesn't work that way, right?
I mean, you need

to have somebody who's
qualified to teach it.
You need to have support.

You need to have a long enough
runway that if you don't get

more than eight or nine
students that first semester,
that the institution still sees it

as valuable to maintain it
until it reaches that, you know,
sort of that critical mass.

And you really kind of need
to have local employers,
the bigger the better,

knocking on the door of
those schools saying,

"If you offer this, if
you train these people,
we will make a point of interviewing them
and possibly hiring them."

So you really need to
have that partnership.
And it happens in places,
but it doesn't happen enough.

- I would agree so much
with that last point.
Something also that I definitely observed
in my time in academia because, you know,
being here in Portland,
we have Intel just 10 miles away.

They have a huge facility here
in Oregon in Hillsborough.

And every time there was a
research fair or a job fair,
guess who shows up?
It's a bunch of people from Intel.
The other thing that we have here

in Portland is a lot of
electron microscope component
and system manufacturers.

And so guess what a lot of
the research was drive around?
Electron imaging, right?
All that kind of stuff, and metrology.
So you have the corporate ecosystem,
they were really heavily involved
in influencing what the university did.
So I agree with you 100%.

The companies that need
people who do PCBs,

they also have to get
involved with the universities
and push them a little bit to get them
to add these kinds of courses
or add people who are qualified in it
to their roles on faculty.

- Again, I mean, I know we're
both in agreement on this
and we're kind of preaching to the choir,

but I think one of the important
elements is that, you know,
